summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

primary_citations.citation_text: Maryland - Md. Code, Family Law Article §§ 5-701 et seq. (Child Abuse and Neglect; definitions at § 5-701, mandatory reporting at §§ 5-704 and 5-705, investigation at § 5-706, appeal of findings at § 5-706.1)
Maryland - Courts & Judicial Proc. § 3-801 et seq. (CINA—Child in Need of Assistance proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Wolf v. Fauquier County Board of Supervisors
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for social services defendants, holding that a parent who complained that a child-abuse investigation was mishandled and unduly prolonged could not show that the investigation fell below the minimum notice-and-opportunity-to-be-heard standards procedural due process requires.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Fourth Circuit's statement of the (low) constitutional floor for the conduct of a CPS investigation.
key_cases.quote: she cannot show that the investigation did not meet the minimum standards required by procedural due process

key_cases.case_name: Horridge v. St. Mary's County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: Reversing dismissal of a wrongful-death complaint, the Court held that FL § 5-706 and its regulations create a mandatory duty owed to the identified child named in an abuse report, so the public duty doctrine does not bar a negligence action against the department and its caseworkers.
key_cases.relevance: It makes prompt on-site investigation of each accepted report a mandatory, non-discretionary duty.
key_cases.quote: This is not an obligation that runs to everyone in general and no one in particular. It runs to an identified or identifiable child or discrete group of children.

key_cases.court: Court of Special Appeals of Maryland
key_cases.holding: The court vacated orders removing reunification from the permanency plan because the juvenile court relied on a polygraph examination, holding that material the department may lawfully use as an investigative tool is not thereby admissible as evidence in an adjudicative proceeding.
key_cases.relevance: It draws the line between what CPS may gather during an investigation and what a court may rely on.
key_cases.quote: we must maintain the careful distinction between an investigative tool and evidence that has sufficient reliability for consideration in an adjudicative proceeding

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for Maryland officials, holding that investigative home visits by social workers are not measured by criminal-search standards and that the entry of the caseworker and accompanying deputies into a consenting foster mother's home was not unreasonable.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Fourth Circuit's Maryland case on the Fourth Amendment standard for CPS home entry during an investigation.
key_cases.quote: investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context

timeline_requirements.deadline: 10 days to the extent possible; if not completed within 30 days, within 60 days
